brief: Morgan Stanley answers investor questions on its prior call sizing a US data center power shortfall at 57 GW gross, 32 GW net of time-to-power fixes, 34% of demand through 2028. Nvidia's own commentary confirms the power constraint is real, but Morgan Stanley stays convicted Nvidia and Broadcom hit their combined ~$800bn 12-month AI revenue outlook, citing management visibility into chip placement, geographic diversification, and Nvidia's higher tokens-per-watt. If a slowdown hits, the firm expects memory, optics and small-dollar components, not Nvidia or Broadcom, to absorb the disruption, with ASICs at risk of losing share to GPUs. Access to power is concentrating among large, credit-worthy hyperscalers and neoclouds, forecast at 60-95% of global data center capacity additions, squeezing smaller, international and ASIC-dependent players; Google's heavy incremental build could make securing power harder for it specifically. Upside depends on behind-the-meter generation (11-49 GW, 19 GW base case) and international expansion, but Morgan Stanley does not see overseas capacity as sufficient to close the US shortfall, cuts its US compute-share estimate to 55% from 60%, and flags labor and political constraints as caps on how fast BTM capacity can scale.
